title: EHRA AI checklist — completed for: Estimating atrial fibrillation burden as a per-patient quantification problem with distribution-free uncertainty intervals
paragraphs: Checklist from: Svennberg E, Han JK, et al. State of the Art of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Electrophysiology in 2025. Europace 2025;27(5):euaf071 (Table 2). Item descriptions are abbreviated; the right-hand column states where each item is addressed in the manuscript. Page numbers to be added by the authors after final typesetting of the submission file.
Reporting standard stated in Methods: TRIPOD+AI and the EHRA AI checklist.

rows: Identify the study as using AI/machine learning
Title ("quantification", "distribution-free"); Abstract Methods name the machine-learning detectors and the hidden Markov quantifier. Authors may wish to add "artificial intelligence" to the title.
Intended use, place in workflow, objective
Introduction (last paragraph); Discussion – Clinical implications: post-processing layer for automated burden from Holter/patch/wearable RR series.
Added benefit vs standard care/gold standard
Introduction; Results – Burden estimation; Discussion – Clinical implications and Limitations (benefit on decisions not tested).
Methods – Data sources; Supplementary Table S1; original database publications cited.
Study design / source of input data
Methods – Study design and Data sources (retrospective, public PhysioNet databases).
Methods – Data sources; Table 1; Supplementary Table S1.

Methods – Data sources and Reference standard (exclusions: invalid RR, unlabelled rhythm, duplicate recording); Table 1. Individual-level demographics not available for most public databases (limitation).
Definition and limitations of ground truth
Methods – Reference standard (database rhythm annotations; AFL counted as non-AF with AF+AFL sensitivity analysis); Discussion – Limitations (annotation quality).
Methods – Data partitioning (patient-level stratified splits, five seeds) and external cohorts never used for training/calibration.
How study size was arrived at
All available annotated patients in each database; Icentia11k random 800-patient subset (computational constraint) – Methods – Data sources; no formal sample-size calculation (limitation).
Methods – Endpoints: per-patient absolute AF-burden error (pp); secondary agreement, threshold classification, coverage.
Methods – Reference standard and units (RR intervals from beat annotations, 0.2–3.0 s, 60-beat windows); Supplementary S2–S3.
Methods – Data partitioning and leakage control; Supplementary S2 (automated duplicate audit; per-window features; calibration sets disjoint). No augmentation used.
Splits stratified by database and AF presence (Methods); no class re-weighting or resampling of windows.

Methods – Reference standard (implausible RR excluded); Supplementary S2 (missing CPSC2021 patient-51 files; duplicate SHDB-AF recording removed; unlabelled Icentia11k segments excluded); robustness to simulated R-peak errors (Results; Figure 5).
Feature selection and who extracted features
Supplementary S3 (16 RR features computed automatically by the authors' code; no data-driven feature selection).
Research software, not approved as a medical device (to be stated by authors in cover letter/Methods if required).

The burden layer is a transparent two-state Markov model with interpretable per-patient transition probabilities; posterior burden and interval are reported per patient (Methods; Supplementary S4). Detectors use interpretable RR features (Classical-LR, LightGBM) or a neural network (RRNet).
Methods – Ethics (public de-identified data; original approvals in cited publications).
External cohorts from Japan, China and Canada; sex and age subgroups in SHDB-AF (Supplementary Table S12); limited demographic metadata elsewhere (limitation).
Data availability statement: all databases public; full code and per-patient results publicly available.
Not applicable (retrospective diagnostic-accuracy study); analysis plan pre-registered in version control (Supplementary S1).
Baseline characteristics of internal and external data
Results – Cohorts; Table 1; Supplementary Figure S1.
RRNet learning curves (Supplementary Figure S4); calibration-B (in-distribution) burden and interval results (Supplementary Table S5).
Development test set results (Table 2, Table 5, Supplementary Table S2).
Window AUROC/AUPRC/sensitivity/specificity/ECE; burden MAE, bias, LoA, CCC, threshold sensitivity/specificity, interval coverage/width.
Results – Error analysis; Figure 6; Supplementary Tables S6, S8, S13; Supplementary Figure S7.
Eight comparators including classical counting, smoothing and statistical quantification estimators (Table 4); classical logistic-regression detector.
Discussion – Interpretation, Comparison with previous work and Limitations.
Conclusions restricted to the measured endpoints; effect size described as modest.
